topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under TREC Rule 1260-02-.07, may a Tennessee broker or affiliate broker accept or enter into a listing agreement based on a "net price" (also known as a net listing)?
choice_a: Yes, provided the seller signs a separate written waiver
choice_b: Yes, but only for commercial property listings
choice_c: No — TREC Rule 1260-02-.07 prohibits a broker or affiliate broker from accepting or entering into a listing based on a net price
choice_d: Yes, net listings are the required standard listing form in Tennessee
explanation: TREC Rule 1260-02-.07 expressly prohibits net listings — an arrangement where the broker keeps everything above a stated net amount to the seller as commission — because they create a conflict of interest that can motivate the broker to withhold higher offers to increase their own compensation.

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under the Tennessee Real Estate Commission's Rules of Conduct, what must every listing agreement form used by a licensee specify regarding its duration?
choice_a: No expiration date is required as long as the seller verbally agrees to a term
choice_b: An automatic indefinite renewal with no end date
choice_c: A minimum term of five years
explanation: The Tennessee Real Estate Commission's Rules of Conduct (Rule 1260-02) prohibit using or promoting a listing agreement form that fails to specify a definite termination date, so that sellers are not bound to an open-ended or indefinite listing obligation.
source_note: TREC Rules of Conduct (Rule 1260-02) — listing agreements must state a definite termination date

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: A seller signs an exclusive right-to-sell listing agreement. If the seller personally finds and sells to a buyer without any involvement from the listing broker, what is the general result under this type of listing?
choice_a: The broker is still entitled to the commission, because an exclusive right-to-sell listing entitles the broker to a commission no matter who procures the buyer
choice_b: The broker is entitled to nothing because the broker was not involved in the sale
choice_c: The listing automatically converts to an open listing once the seller finds a buyer
choice_d: The seller can never sell the property to anyone during the listing period
explanation: Under an exclusive right-to-sell listing, the broker earns a commission regardless of who actually procures the buyer — including the seller — which distinguishes it from an exclusive agency listing (where the seller may sell without owing a commission if the seller personally procures the buyer) or an open listing.
source_note: General real estate brokerage listing-agreement principles — exclusive right-to-sell listings

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: A broker tells a seller they are signing an "open listing," allowing the seller to also list with other brokers or sell the home independently, but the document the seller actually signs is an exclusive right-to-sell agreement. What kind of violation does this represent?
choice_a: No violation, because all listing agreement types are functionally identical
choice_b: Improper, fraudulent, or dishonest dealing in connection with the listing agreement, which is grounds for discipline under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)
choice_c: A violation only if the seller ultimately sells the property to a third party
choice_d: A violation only if the commission rate exceeds 6%
explanation: Misrepresenting the nature of a listing agreement a seller is signing is a form of improper, fraudulent, or dishonest dealing, which T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b) identifies as grounds for the Tennessee Real Estate Commission to discipline a licensee's license.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(20) — improper, fraudulent, or dishonest dealing

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under the Tennessee Human Rights Act's housing provisions, codified at T.C.A. § 4-21-601 and following, what is generally prohibited?
choice_a: Charging any application fee whatsoever to a prospective tenant
choice_c: Discriminatory housing practices in the sale, rental, financing, or advertising of housing based on protected characteristics
choice_d: Requiring a credit check as part of a rental application
explanation: T.C.A. § 4-21-601, part of the Tennessee Human Rights Act's discrimination-in-housing-and-financing provisions, makes it unlawful to engage in discriminatory housing practices — including in sales, rentals, financing, and advertising — based on protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, and familial status.
source_note: T.C.A. § 4-21-601 — Tennessee Human Rights Act, discriminatory housing practices generally

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: For a Tennessee real estate licensee, how does violating a fair housing discrimination law affect their real estate license under the Tennessee Real Estate Broker License Act?
choice_a: It has no effect on the licensee's real estate license, only on any separate civil lawsuit
choice_b: It results in automatic permanent revocation with no hearing rights, regardless of severity
choice_c: It is only a violation if a criminal conviction results
choice_d: It is expressly listed as a ground for discipline — violating any federal, state, or municipal law prohibiting discrimination in the sale or rental of real estate
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b) lists violating any federal, state, or municipal law prohibiting discrimination in the sale or rental of real estate as one of the specific grounds on which the Tennessee Real Estate Commission may refuse, suspend, or revoke a license.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(13) — discrimination as grounds for discipline

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Which of the following characteristics are protected under Tennessee's housing discrimination law, in addition to race, color, religion, sex, and national origin?
explanation: Consistent with federal fair housing law, Tennessee's housing discrimination provisions under the Tennessee Human Rights Act also protect against discrimination based on disability and familial status, in addition to race, color, religion, sex, and national origin.
source_note: T.C.A. § 4-21-601 et seq. — Tennessee Human Rights Act, protected classes in housing

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: A licensee only shows a buyer of a particular protected class properties in certain neighborhoods, steering the buyer away from other areas the buyer expressed interest in. What is this practice called, and how is it treated?
choice_a: Steering — a legitimate marketing strategy a broker may freely choose to use
choice_b: Steering — an illegal discriminatory housing practice under T.C.A. § 4-21-601 and grounds for license discipline under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)
choice_c: Blockbusting — but only illegal if done in writing
choice_d: A permissible practice as long as the buyer does not complain
explanation: Steering — limiting or directing a buyer's or tenant's housing choices based on a protected characteristic — is a form of discriminatory housing practice prohibited by the Tennessee Human Rights Act, and it also exposes the licensee to discipline under the Tennessee Real Estate Broker License Act.
source_note: T.C.A. § 4-21-601 and T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(13) — steering as unlawful discrimination

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b), "making any substantial and willful misrepresentation" in a real estate transaction is treated as what?
choice_a: A minor infraction that can never result in discipline
choice_b: Grounds for discipline only if the misrepresentation is made in writing
choice_c: Grounds for the Tennessee Real Estate Commission to refuse, suspend, or revoke a license
choice_d: Grounds for discipline only against a principal broker, never an affiliate broker
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(1) lists making a substantial and willful misrepresentation as one of the specific statutory grounds allowing the commission to discipline a licensee, regardless of whether the licensee is an affiliate broker or principal broker.

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b), what is the disciplinary consequence for a licensee who pays or accepts an undisclosed commission, rebate, or compensation in connection with a real estate transaction?
choice_a: It is permitted as long as it is not reported on the licensee's tax return
choice_b: It is only a violation if the amount exceeds $10,000
choice_c: It is not addressed anywhere in Tennessee real estate law
choice_d: It is grounds for the commission to discipline the licensee's license
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(17) makes paying, accepting, giving, or charging any undisclosed commission, rebate, compensation, or profit to or from a principal, in violation of the chapter, a specific ground for discipline against a licensee's real estate license.

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: A listing broker in Tennessee wants to purchase the very property they have listed for a seller-client. Under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b), what must the broker do to avoid a licensing violation?
choice_a: Disclose to the seller the broker's own interest in and intent to purchase the listed property
choice_b: Nothing; brokers are always free to purchase their own listings without disclosure
choice_c: Wait until after the listing agreement expires, which removes any disclosure obligation
choice_d: Obtain approval only from the Tennessee Real Estate Commission, not the seller
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(18) makes it a ground for discipline to fail to disclose to a party being represented the licensee's own interest in, or intent to purchase, the listed property. A broker wanting to buy their own listing must disclose this self-interest to the seller before proceeding.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(18) — failure to disclose licensee's interest in purchasing listed property

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b), how long must a Tennessee licensee preserve records relating to a real estate transaction, and what happens if they fail to do so?
choice_a: There is no minimum record retention period under Tennessee real estate law
choice_b: Three years; failing to preserve such records for that period is grounds for discipline
choice_c: Ten years, matching the federal tax records retention period
choice_d: Only until closing occurs, after which records may be destroyed immediately
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(6) makes it a disciplinable offense for a licensee to fail to preserve records relating to any real estate transaction for at least three years, ensuring transaction documentation remains available for later review by the commission or the parties.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(6) — failure to preserve transaction records

topic: Other Improper Activities and Consumer Protection
question: Under T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b), a licensee who acts on behalf of more than one party to the same real estate transaction (for example, representing both buyer and seller) without obtaining what may face discipline?
choice_a: A verbal acknowledgment from just one of the parties
choice_b: Approval from a competing brokerage firm
choice_c: The written consent of all parties to the transaction
choice_d: A separate real estate license for each party represented
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(7) makes it grounds for discipline to act for more than one party in a transaction without the written consent of all parties involved, addressing dual agency and similar conflicts of interest.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-312(b)(7) — acting for multiple parties without written consent
